In the paper arXiv:1611.01958v5, Taras Bodnar, Yarema Okhrin, and Nestor Parolya propose a linear shrinkage estimator designed to address this high-dimensional breakdown. The method uses random matrix theory to account for the estimation risk in the sample mean vector. This is a structural correction for the noise that typically enters the optimization when the asset dimension exceeds the available observations.

  This shifts the focus from merely correcting the covariance matrix to addressing the joint estimation error of the mean and the variance. If the mean vector is treated as a fixed truth rather than a noisy estimate, the resulting weights will always overfit the sample noise.

  The Bodnar estimator corrects this by treating the mean vector not as a point estimate, but as a random variable with a known distribution of error. By applying a linear shrinkage $\\hat{\\mu} {shrink} = (1-\\lambda)\\hat{\\mu} + \\lambda \\mu {target}$, where $\\lambda$ is derived from Random Matrix Theory (RMT), the estimator explicitly accounts for the estimation risk. For a practitioner, the concrete advantage here is the reduction in the variance of the weight vector. In cases where $p  n$, the sample covariance matrix is singular and non-invertible; the Bodnar approach provides a regularization path that allows for a stable solution without the arbitrary nature of Tikhonov regularization or simple diagonal loading.

### Key Contributions

Proposed novel filtering methods based on tensor decompositions for high-order co-moment estimation, significantly improving out-of-sample accuracy for large-scale portfolio risk management.

### Abstract

Portfolio risk is not limited to the variance of returns. The moments of portfolio returns depend directly on the covariance matrix and higher-order co-dependences (coskewness, cokurtosis, etc.). In practice, however, these objects are extremely noisy, especially for large portfolios. Here we introduce filtering methods based on tensor decompositions that extend cross-validated covariance cleaning and the Average Oracle methodology to even-order co-moment tensors. Using returns on historical Russell 1000 constituents, we find that the proposed filters improve out-of-sample estimation accuracy relative to sample estimators, both for correlation and cokurtosis tensors, as measured by relative squared Frobenius errors. These improvements translate into lower relative errors on portfolio volatility and kurtosis, and into lower out-of-sample volatility and kurtosis when the portfolio objective penalizes both variance and the fourth moment.

### Summary

This paper introduces tensor-based filtering methods to improve the estimation accuracy of high-order co-moment tensors in large portfolios, effectively reducing noise in risk assessment.

context.snippet: ## Related works ### Covariance estimation methods The estimation of covariance matrices is a fundamental problem in statistics and machine learning. The sample covariance matrix, while straightforward, often performs poorly in high-dimensional settings because of its susceptibility to ill- conditioned4. To address this issue, Ledoit and Wolf (2004)5 proposed a linear shrinkage estimator that shrinks the sample covariance matrix toward a target matrix and optimizes the shrinkage intensity to minimize the mean squared error. This method significantly improves the conditioning of the covariance matrix, ensuring its invertibility and stability, even in high-dimensional settings. Building on this work, Ledoit and Wolf (2015)6 introduced a nonlinear shrinkage estimator that adaptively adjusts the shrinkage intensity of each eigenvalue based on its position in the spectrum. This nonlinear method further enhances estimation accuracy and computational efficiency, particularly in applications such as portfolio optimization and principal component analysis. Empirical results demonstrate that the nonlinear shrinkage estimator outperforms both the sample covariance matrix and linear shrinkage methods, achieving superior performance in terms of out-of-sample portfolio returns and risk management. Building on the above research, traditional nonlinear methods (such as QuEST and NERCOME) rely on numerical computations or sample splitting, which are inefficient and struggle to handle ultra-high-dimensional data. Ledoit and Wolf (2020)7 developed an analytical nonlinear shrinkage method that combines efficiency, accuracy, and theoretical elegance, breaking through dimensional limitations and improving computational speed. Their core innovation–the combination of the Hilbert transform and kernel estimation–provides a new paradigm for interdisciplinary research in random matrix theory, nonparametric estimation, and high-dimensional statistics.

            Abstract:Portfolio risk is not limited to the variance of returns. The moments of portfolio returns depend directly on the covariance matrix and higher-order co-dependences (coskewness, cokurtosis, etc.). In practice, however, these objects are extremely noisy, especially for large portfolios. Here we introduce filtering methods based on tensor decompositions that extend cross-validated covariance cleaning and the Average Oracle methodology to even-order co-moment tensors. Using returns on historical Russell 1000 constituents, we find that the proposed filters improve out-of-sample estimation accuracy relative to sample estimators, both for correlation and cokurtosis tensors, as measured by relative squared Frobenius errors. These improvements translate into lower relative errors on portfolio volatility and kurtosis, and into lower out-of-sample volatility and kurtosis when the portfolio objective penalizes both variance and the fourth moment.

While linear shrinkage works well if the eigenvalues of the true covariance matrix are not too dispersed, as every sample eigenvalue is shrunken by the same amount, NL shrinkage is able to adapt to more dispersed eigenvalues, by allowing for different shrinkage intensities for each sample eigenvalue. Owing to the above mentioned implicit connection to a Gaussian likelihood, we denote estimation with the sample mean and NL shrinkage applied to the covariance matrix as the MN-NL, or MN-IID-NL model to explicitly stress the i.i.d. assumption. This model allows for quick estimation and portfolio selection in hundreds or even thousands of dimensions, while at the same time inheriting the strong performance of the Gaussian–Markowitz approach for a “small” amount of assets. It is hard to understate what an extremely strong benchmark this relatively simple model constitutes, especially in net returns. In particular, the analysis of De Nard et al. (2019) indicates a strong improvement of MN-IID-NL over the Fama–French five-factor model in portfolio selection.

In addition, NL shrinkage was recently combined with the Dynamical Conditional Correlation (DCC) approach of Engle (2002) in Engle et al. (2019), hereafter called DCC-NL model. # Nonlinear Shrinkage Estimation of Higher-Order Moments for Portfolio Optimization Under Uncertainty in Complex

1School of Management Science and Engineering, Southwestern University of Finance and Economics, Chengdu 611130, China.

Abstract:

This paper develops a nonlinear shrinkage estimation method for higher-order moment matrices within a multifactor model framework and establishes its asymptotic consistency under high-dimensional settings. The approach extends the nonlinear shrinkage methodology from covariance to higher-order moments, thereby mitigating the "curse of dimensionality" and alleviating estimation uncertainty in high-dimensional settings. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate that, compared with linear shrinkage estimation, the proposed method substantially reduces mean squared errors (MSEs) and achieves greater Percentage Relative Improvement in Average Loss (PRIAL) for covariance and cokurtosis estimates; relative to sample estimation, it delivers significant gains in mitigating uncertainty for covariance, coskewness, and cokurtosis. An empirical portfolio analysis incorporating higher-order moments shows that, when the asset universe is large, portfolios based on the nonlinear shrinkage estimator outperform those constructed using linear shrinkage and sample estimators, achieving higher annualized return and Sharpe ratio with lower kurtosis and maximum drawdown, thus providing stronger resilience against uncertainty in complex financial systems. In smaller asset universes, nonlinear shrinkage portfolios perform on par with their linear shrinkage counterparts. These findings highlight the potential of nonlinear shrinkage techniques to reduce uncertainty in higher-order moment estimation and to improve portfolio performance across diverse and complex investment environments.

deepseek.title: Higher-Moment Portfolio Optimization with Shrinkage Estimators
deepseek.snippet:
This thesis investigates whether reducing the estimation error of higher-order co-moments through shrinkage improves the out-of-sample performance of portfolios that account for skewness and kurtosis, and under which conditions such improvements arise. Building on the mean–variance–skewness–kurtosis framework, portfolio weights are obtained by maximising a fourth-order Taylor expansion of a constant relative risk aversion utility, so that the investor's preference for positive skewness and aversion to fat tails are made explicit. The co-skewness and co-kurtosis matrices are estimated using single-factor shrinkage targets in the spirit of Martellini and Ziemann (2010), combined with Ledoit–Wolf shrinkage of the covariance matrix. A central methodological contribution is the selection of the shrinkage intensity by cross-validation rather than by the usual closed-form rule, which proves unstable in this setting. The estimators are evaluated in a rolling-window backtest, net of transaction costs, across two distinct asset universes, a set of cryptocurrencies and a multi-asset universe, and their performance is assessed through risk-adjusted and utility-based metrics together with formal tests of statistical significance. The analysis clarifies when shrinkage of higher-order co-moments delivers economically and statistically meaningful gains, and when estimation error and portfolio concentration render competing estimators indistinguishable.

# Nonlinear Shrinkage for Higher Moments Estimation in Large Portfolios

Portfolio risk is not limited to the variance of returns. The moments of portfolio returns depend directly on the covariance matrix and higher-order co-dependences (coskewness, cokurtosis, etc.). In practice, however, these objects are extremely noisy, especially for large portfolios. Here we introduce filtering methods based on tensor decompositions that extend cross-validated covariance cleaning and the Average Oracle methodology to even-order co-moment tensors. Using returns on historical Russell 1000 constituents, we find that the proposed filters improve out-of-sample estimation accuracy relative to sample estimators, both for correlation and cokurtosis tensors, as measured by relative squared Frobenius errors. These improvements translate into lower relative errors on portfolio volatility and kurtosis, and into lower out-of-sample volatility and kurtosis when the portfolio objective penalizes both variance and the fourth moment.

keenable.title: Shrinkage Estimation of Covariance Matrix for Portfolio Choice with High Frequency Data
keenable.snippet:
This paper examines the usefulness of high frequency data in estimating the covariance matrix for portfolio choice when the portfolio size is large. A computationally convenient nonlinear shrinkage estimator for the integrated covariance (ICV) matrix of financial assets is developed in two steps. The eigenvectors of the ICV are first constructed from a designed time variation adjusted realized covariance matrix of noise-free log-returns of relatively low frequency data. Then the regularized eigenvalues of the ICV are estimated by quasi-maximum likelihood based on high frequency data. The estimator is always positive definite and its inverse is the estimator of the inverse of ICV. It minimizes the limit of the out-of-sample variance of portfolio returns within the class of rotation-equivalent estimators. It works when the number of underlying assets is larger than the number of time series observations in each asset and when the asset price follows a general stochastic process. Our theoretical results are derived under the assumption that the number of assets (p) and the sample size (n) satisfy p/n→y>0 as n→∞. The advantages of our proposed estimator are demonstrated using real data.

We estimate covariance matrices that are tailored to portfolio optimisation con-
straints. We rely on a generalised version of James–Stein for eigenvectors (JSE),
a data-driven operator that reduces estimation error in the leading sample eigen-
vector by shrinking towards a target subspace determined by constraint gradients.

constraints.

Shrinkage operators dampen the effects of extreme observations in data sets, which
occur routinely in ﬁnance. The concept of shrinkage dates back at least to Stein [68]
and James and Stein [38] in the 1950s and 1960s. They show that in dimension 3
or greater, the sample average is inadmissible: there is another estimator with lower
mean-squared error. That superior estimator is known as James–Stein, and it is ob-

extended by replacing the collective average with arbitrary initial guesses in Efron
and Morris [20], and popularised by Efron [21]. An overview of James–Stein type
shrinkage estimation is in Foudrinier et al. [26, Chap. 2].

An advanced evolution of the linear Ledoit-Wolf framework, **nonlinear shrinkage** applies a unique intensity to each eigenvalue of the sample covariance matrix rather than a single global parameter.  
- **Eigenvalue Clustering**: Sample eigenvalues are often over-dispersed; large eigenvalues are estimated too high and small ones too low.

- **High-Dimensional Superiority**: This method is asymptotically optimal when the concentration ratio (N/T) is high, making it the state-of-the-art for large-scale portfolio construction with thousands of assets.
Covariance shrinkage is a statistical estimation technique that combines a **sample covariance matrix** (computed directly from historical return data) with a highly structured **target matrix** (such as the constant correlation or identity matrix) to produce a more stable estimator. The process works by computing a weighted average: `Σ_shrunk = δ * T + (1 - δ) * S`, where `S` is the sample matrix, `T` is the target, and `δ` (delta) is the shrinkage intensity between 0 and 1. # Nonlinear Shrinkage for Higher Moments Estimation in Large Portfolios

arXiv:2611.27274
Authors: Paul Ruelloux, Christian Bongiorno, Damien Challet
Submitted: 2026-11-20
Subjects: q-fin.PM q-fin.RM q-fin.ST
Comments: 30 pages, 6 figures, including Supplementary Information. An earlier conference version circulated under the title "Higher-Order Moment Shrinkage for Risk Assessment"

Abstract

Portfolio risk is not limited to the variance of returns. The moments of portfolio returns depend directly on the covariance matrix and higher-order co-dependences (coskewness, cokurtosis, etc.). In practice, however, these objects are extremely noisy, especially for large portfolios. Here we introduce filtering methods based on tensor decompositions that extend cross-validated covariance cleaning and the Average Oracle methodology to even-order co-moment tensors. Using returns on historical Russell 1000 constituents, we find that the proposed filters improve out-of-sample estimation accuracy relative to sample estimators, both for correlation and cokurtosis tensors, as measured by relative squared Frobenius errors. These improvements translate into lower relative errors on portfolio volatility and kurtosis, and into lower out-of-sample volatility and kurtosis when the portfolio objective penalizes both variance and the fourth moment.

## Abstract

This paper develops a nonlinear shrinkage estimation method for higher-order moment matrices within a multifactor model framework and establishes its asymptotic consistency under high-dimensional settings. MENS: Nonlinear Shrinkage Estimation in Nonparanormal Models for Financial Applications
Abstract
We develop a theory of nonlinear shrinkage covariance estimation for nonparanormal (Gaussian-copula) models, in which each observed coordinate is an unknown strictly increasing transformation of a latent Gaussian vector. This model accommodates arbitrary marginal skewness and heavy marginal tails while retaining a Gaussian dependence structure, and it is the natural semiparametric setting for heavy-tailed, asymmetric financial returns. Our estimator, marginal-free nonlinear shrinkage (MENS), applies an oracle nonlinear shrinkage function to the eigenvalues of the normal-scores rank-covariance matrix. We give the almost-sure convergence of the empirical spectral distribution of the normal-scores covariance to the generalized Marčenko–Pastur law of , and asymptotic optimality of MENS among rotation-equivariant estimators under Frobenius loss. We establish a Baik–Ben Arous–Péché phase transition for spiked latent correlations. The MENS attains the robustness of rank-based estimation and the efficiency of nonlinear shrinkage at once within this class. We corroborate the theory with a simulation study that isolates the marginal-invariance property and the spiked transition. In an out-of-sample minimum-variance backtest on S&P 500 stocks, MENS delivers a better-conditioned covariance estimate, lower realized portfolio volatility, and lower turnover than linear shrinkage, illustrating its practical value for high-dimensional allocation and decision-making.

Abstract
Many statistical applications require an estimate of a covariance matrix and/or its inverse. Whenthe matrix dimension is large compared to the sample size, which happens frequently, the samplecovariance matrix is known to perform poorly and may suffer from ill-conditioning. There alreadyexists an extensive literature concerning improved estimators in such situations. In the absence offurther knowledge about the structure of the true covariance matrix, the most successful approachso far, arguably, has been shrinkage estimation. Shrinking the sample covariance matrix to amultiple of the identity, by taking a weighted average of the two, turns out to be equivalent tolinearly shrinking the sample eigenvalues to their grand mean, while retaining the sampleeigenvectors. Our paper extends this approach by considering nonlinear transformations of thesample eigenvalues. We show how to construct an estimator that is asymptotically equivalent toan oracle estimator suggested in previous work. As demonstrated in extensive Monte Carlosimulations, the resulting bona fide estimator can result in sizeable improvements over the samplecovariance matrix and also over linear shrinkage.

Give an optimiser a covariance matrix for 100 stocks built from six months of daily returns and it will hand back a portfolio it believes is very safe. It is not. ## Covariance Matrices in Portfolio Optimization

If there is one mathematical object that sits at the absolute centre of modern portfolio theory, it is the covariance matrix. It is the object that encodes how assets move relative to one another — whether they rise and fall together, move in opposite directions, or behave independently. Every portfolio optimisation, every risk decomposition, every hedge ratio, and every stress test depends on an accurate characterisation of these pairwise relationships. Get the covariance matrix right, and the optimiser builds portfolios with genuinely diversified risk. Get it wrong — as happens far more often than practitioners acknowledge — and the resulting portfolios are fragile, concentrated in hidden ways, and prone to catastrophic drawdowns precisely when diversification is needed most.

This blog is a deep dive into the covariance matrix in the context of portfolio optimisation. It covers the mathematical foundations, the statistical challenges of estimation from finite data, the computational mechanics of using it in optimisation, the major estimation methodologies employed by institutional quant funds, and the practical failure modes that every quantitative analyst must understand. ## Why This Matters

Covariance matrices are everywhere: PCA, factor models, portfolio optimization, Gaussian processes, linear discriminant analysis. All of these methods require a covariance estimate. In low dimensions (n≫dn \gg d), the sample covariance matrix works well. In high dimensions (dd comparable to or larger than nn), it fails catastrophically: eigenvalues spread out, the matrix may be singular, and the estimation error in operator norm does not even converge to zero.

This is not an academic concern. Gene expression data has d∼20,000d \sim 20{,}000 genes and n∼100n \sim 100 samples. Financial returns data has d∼500d \sim 500 stocks and n∼250n \sim 250 trading days. In both cases, dd is comparable to or exceeds nn, and the sample covariance is useless without regularization.

The sample covariance matrix is the "plug-in" estimator: replace the population expectation with a sample average. When n≫dn \gg d, this works by the law of large numbers. When n≈dn \approx d, the sample covariance has d2d^2 free parameters but only ndnd data points to estimate them. The estimation problem is underdetermined, and the sample eigenvalues systematically spread away from the true eigenvalues (the Marcenko-Pastur phenomenon).

### Abstract

Many machine learning algorithms require precise estimates of covariance matrices. The sample covariance matrix performs poorly in high-dimensional settings, which has stimulated the development of alternative methods, the majority based on factor models and shrinkage. Recent work of Ledoit and Wolf has extended the shrinkage framework to Nonlinear Shrinkage (NLS), a more powerful covariance estimator

Our contribution shows that, contrary to claims in the literature, cross-validation based covariance matrix estimation (CVC) yields comparable performance at strongly reduced complexity and runtime. On two real world data sets, we show that the CVC estimator yields superior results than competing shrinkage and factor

based methods.

### 1 Introduction

## Modern Portfolio Theory (MPT) Explained

Few ideas have reshaped finance as profoundly as Modern Portfolio Theory. When Harry Markowitz published his seminal paper in the Journal of Finance in 1952, he introduced a framework that transformed portfolio construction from an art guided by intuition and heuristic rules into a rigorous mathematical discipline grounded in probability theory and optimisation. The central insight was deceptively simple: the risk of a portfolio is not the average of the risks of its constituent assets, because assets do not move in perfect lockstep. Diversification across imperfectly correlated assets reduces portfolio risk without proportionally reducing expected return, and this reduction can be quantified precisely and exploited systematically. From this foundation, Markowitz built an optimisation framework that identifies the set of portfolios offering the maximum expected return for any given level of risk, a construct he called the efficient frontier. The decades following the 1952 paper saw MPT extended, challenged, and refined by a generation of financial economists, producing the Capital Asset Pricing Model, the Arbitrage Pricing Theory, and eventually the factor model revolution that now dominates institutional investment practice. This post develops MPT from its mathematical foundations through its practical implementation, examining both its enduring insights and its well-documented limitations.

## Optimization Algorithms for Portfolio Management

Portfolio management is, at its mathematical heart, an optimization problem. Given a universe of assets, each with uncertain future returns, and given an investor with preferences over wealth outcomes, the portfolio manager must select weights that are in some sense optimal — maximizing return for a given level of risk, minimizing risk for a given level of return, or maximizing some utility function that captures the investor's attitude toward the trade-off between the two. This seemingly simple objective conceals extraordinary complexity: the objective functions are often non-convex, the constraints are numerous and heterogeneous, the inputs are estimated with substantial uncertainty, and the dimensionality of the problem grows with the number of assets, easily reaching thousands in institutional portfolios.

# Nonlinear Shrinkage for Higher Moments Estimation in Large Portfolios

Portfolio risk is not limited to the variance of returns. The moments of portfolio returns depend directly on the covariance matrix and higher-order co-dependences (coskewness, cokurtosis, etc.). In practice, however, these objects are extremely noisy, especially for large portfolios. Here we introduce filtering methods based on tensor decompositions that extend cross-validated covariance cleaning and the Average Oracle methodology to even-order co-moment tensors. Using returns on historical Russell 1000 constituents, we find that the proposed filters improve out-of-sample estimation accuracy relative to sample estimators, both for correlation and cokurtosis tensors, as measured by relative squared Frobenius errors. These improvements translate into lower relative errors on portfolio volatility and kurtosis, and into lower out-of-sample volatility and kurtosis when the portfolio objective penalizes both variance and the fourth moment.

ultimate.snippet: This paper develops a nonlinear shrinkage estimation method for higher-order moment matrices within a multifactor model framework and establishes its asymptotic consistency under high-dimensional settings. The approach extends the nonlinear shrinkage methodology from covariance to higher-order moments, thereby mitigating the “curse of dimensionality” and alleviating estimation uncertainty in high-dimensional settings. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate that, compared with linear shrinkage estimation, the proposed method substantially reduces mean squared errors (MSEs) and achieves greater Percentage Relative Improvement in Average Loss (PRIAL) for covariance and cokurtosis estimates; relative to sample estimation, it delivers significant gains in mitigating uncertainty for covariance, coskewness, and cokurtosis. In smaller asset universes, nonlinear shrinkage portfolios perform on par with their linear shrinkage counterparts. These findings highlight the potential of nonlinear shrinkage techniques to reduce uncertainty in higher-order moment estimation and to improve portfolio performance across diverse and complex investment environments.

ultimate.title: MENS: Nonlinear Shrinkage Estimation in Nonparanormal Models for Financial Applications
ultimate.snippet: We develop a theory of nonlinear shrinkage covariance estimation for nonparanormal (Gaussian-copula) models, in which each observed coordinate is an unknown strictly increasing transformation of a latent Gaussian vector. This model accommodates arbitrary marginal skewness and heavy marginal tails while retaining a Gaussian dependence structure, and it is the natural semiparametric setting for heavy-tailed, asymmetric financial returns. Our estimator, marginal-free nonlinear shrinkage (MENS), applies an oracle nonlinear shrinkage function to the eigenvalues of the normal-scores rank-covariance matrix. We give the almost-sure convergence of the empirical spectral distribution of the normal-scores covariance to the generalized Marčenko–Pastur law of 𝚺, and asymptotic optimality of MENS among rotation-equivariant estimators under Frobenius loss. We establish a Baik–Ben Arous–Péché phase transition for spiked latent correlations. The MENS attains the robustness of rank-based estimation and the efficiency of nonlinear shrinkage at once within this class. We corroborate the theory with a simulation study that isolates the marginal-invariance property and the spiked transition. In an out-of-sample minimum-variance backtest on S&P 500 stocks, MENS delivers a better-conditioned covariance estimate, lower realized portfolio volatility, and lower turnover than linear shrinkage, illustrating its practical value for high-dimensional allocation and decision-making.

We estimate covariance matrices that are tailored to portfolio optimisation con-
straints. We rely on a generalised version of James–Stein for eigenvectors (JSE),
a data-driven operator that reduces estimation error in the leading sample eigen-
vector by shrinking towards a target subspace determined by constraint gradients.
Unchecked, this error gives rise to excess volatility for optimised portfolios. Our
results include a formula for the asymptotic improvement of JSE over the leading
sample eigenvector as an estimate of ground truth, and provide improved optimal

2.4 James–Stein shrinkage for averages and for eigenvectors
Shrinkage operators dampen the effects of extreme observations in data sets, which
occur routinely in ﬁnance. The concept of shrinkage dates back at least to Stein [68]
and James and Stein [38] in the 1950s and 1960s. They show that in dimension 3
or greater, the sample average is inadmissible: there is another estimator with lower
mean-squared error. That superior estimator is known as James–Stein, and it is ob-
tained by shrinking sample averages towards their collective average. This work was
extended by replacing the collective average with arbitrary initial guesses in Efron
and Morris [20], and popularised by Efron [21]. An overview of James–Stein type
shrinkage estimation is in Foudrinier et al. [26, Chap. 2].
